summary: Nanjing University authors argue that explicit usability requirements make coding models drop implicit security. U-SPLOIT picks function-level tasks the model already solves securely, has an auxiliary model invent functionality, implementation, or trade-off pressures, and scores a regression if functional tests still pass but a security test or a model-written payload fails. Headline rates are on the Python slice of 75 CWEval and SeCodePLT scenarios.

claims.claim: Usability pressure reaches attack success up to 98.1% on GPT-5.2-chat and similarly high rates on other frontier models
claims.evidence: Table 2, Python, temperature 0, after up to three synthesis rounds: Type 3 ASR is 98.1% (GPT-5.2, baseline 54/75), 94.4% (Gemini-3-Flash, 55/75), 97.2% (DeepSeek-V3.2, 37/75), 91.7% (GPT-5.1, 49/75). Type 3 is defined as an explicit security-versus-usability trade-off. §5.4 says these prompts often push the model to disable a security control outright. The stealthier Type 2 band is 56.4–61.2%.

claims.claim: Security-compatible functionality pressure still induces insecure code at about 82–86% ASR
claims.evidence: Table 2 Type 1: 81.8–85.7% of already-secure Python baselines. The authors require a secure solution to exist and say the judge rejects prompts that demand insecure code. There is no human audit of that filter, and success can be declared by an LLM-written payload when benchmark tests do not fire (Table 5: 36.8% of Type 1 detections).

claims.claim: The effect holds across C and JavaScript as well as Python
claims.evidence: Table 4 is Gemini-3-Flash only. Baseline secure rates are 73.3% Python, 65.3% JavaScript, 52.0% C. Type 3 ASR stays above 93% in all three. No Java. Main tables are Python only.

claims.claim: Repeating synthesis and dynamic payloads are necessary pieces of the measured success
claims.evidence: Fig. 5: Type 1 ASR grows from 51.3% to 83.6% across attempts (+32.3 points); Type 3 starts at 83.1% and adds 10.8 points. Table 5, Gemini Python: dynamic payloads account for 55.8% of Type 2 detections and 9.3% of Type 3. Payloads are produced by the same Gemini analyzer used as a victim model, with no human exploit validation.

patterns.note: Adding an explicit usability requirement to a task the model already solved securely drops security (Table 2). That isolates the extra requirement text. The paper never tests the remedy of writing the security constraint as an acceptance criterion, so it does not show that structured requirements prevent the drop. Type 3 is an explicit instruction to relax security, which is a different intervention from a normal feature request.

Existing security tests miss a large share of Type 1 and Type 2 regressions that the authors count only after a model-written payload (Table 5). The tests are necessary and incomplete. The extra detector is itself an unvalidated LLM.
Gemini-3-Flash analyzes the secure solution and writes payloads; GPT-5.2 judges whether a pressure is too obvious. Both models are also victims. No human agreement is reported.
The threat story is a developer forwarding an issue without asking whether security still holds. Clarifying questions are not tested.

methodology.sample: 75 seed scenarios, 25 CWEs times 3 cases, drawn from CWEval and SeCodePLT and rewritten to a shared I/O format. ASR is computed only on the subset the victim already solved securely (37–55 of 75 on Python).
methodology.baselines: Original task specification with no added pressure. Transfer uses the 33 cases all four models solved securely. No defense is evaluated in the main experiment.
methodology.models: Victims: GPT-5.1-chat, GPT-5.2-chat, Gemini-3-Flash-Preview, DeepSeek-V3.2. Analyzer: Gemini-3-Flash-Preview. Judge: GPT-5.2-chat.
methodology.variance: Victim temperature 0, so one sample per final prompt. Attack synthesis temperature 1 with up to three rounds and three payload retries. No seeds and no intervals.
methodology.ablations: Three pressure types, multi-round search (Fig. 5), and benchmark tests versus dynamic payloads (Table 5). No ablation that adds an explicit security acceptance criterion.
methodology.contamination_controls: None stated. Tasks come from public secure-coding benchmarks.
methodology.languages: Python for the main tables; C and JavaScript for Gemini only. No Java.

standards.artifacts: Impact statement says artifacts will be anonymized during review and released after acceptance. No repository is given.

biases.detail: The abstract's 'realistic usability' and 'silently dropping' story is carried by the 98% figure, which is Type 3: prompts that frame security as the thing to give up, often by disabling a control.
Security regressions can be declared by an analyzer-written payload. The analyzer is a victim model. No human check of exploit validity or of the 'not too obvious' filter.
Gemini-3-Flash both crafts pressures and payloads and is scored as a target. GPT-5.2 both judges prompt validity and is scored as a target.
Single-function completions with bundled tests, not repository changes, issue threads, or multi-file patches.
Only tasks the model already got right and secure are attacked, and the attacker may retry synthesis. ASR is not the rate at which a single natural feature request fails.
One victim sample per prompt. Reported rates have no interval.
Tasks, pressures, and payloads are not released.
Headline tables are Python. The language table is one model. Java is absent.

coi.affiliations: Nanjing University, Shandong University, Nanyang Technological University
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Third-party chat models only. No author product.
coi.detail: Academic security study. No vendor affiliation in the author block.

verdict_reason: The controlled comparison is real: on tasks a model already solved securely, extra requirement text often yields functionally passing but less secure code, including when the authors claim a secure implementation still exists. The 98% headline is the explicit trade-off arm, payloads are model-judged, tasks are tiny, and nothing is released. Treat Type 2 (about 56–61%) as the number closest to a bland engineering constraint.
applicability: For spec-driven work, an explicit feature, latency, or simplicity line can override security the model was not asked to keep. Acceptance criteria for ingestion and delivery changes should name the security properties that must survive (input handling, auth, crypto, resource limits), and review should not treat green functional tests as a security check. The result is function-level Python, C, and JavaScript, not a Java multi-repo change, and it does not test whether writing the security rule into the spec actually stops the drop.
